title: Personal finance: making ends meet
subtitle: broke, strapped for cash, a lump sum, in debt
summary: Talk about your own money - being broke or rolling in it, paying by direct debit or card, and the savings, pensions and investments that make up personal finance.

lesson.heading: Having money - and not having it
lesson.text: English has a whole scale of informal expressions for the state of your finances. **Broke** is informal and **skint** is very informal; both mean you have no money left. At the other end, if you are **rolling in it** you have plenty.

examples.text: I was **broke**/**skint** at the end of last month.
I'm **rolling in it** this month; I got a payment of 3,000 pounds for some work I did.
examples.note: rolling in it = have a lot of money (informal)

examples.text: It's sometimes difficult to **make ends meet** with three children and only one parent working.

lesson.heading: When money is short
lesson.text: Two useful informal phrases describe a temporary shortage. If things are **tight**, your finances are not good at the moment. If you are **strapped for cash**, you need money and have very little.

examples.text: Things are a bit **tight** at the moment.
I was **strapped for cash** and had to borrow money from my parents.
She gave me a cheque for what she owed me but it **bounced**.
examples.note: bounced = the bank refused to pay it

lesson.heading: Paying: cheques, transfers and cards
lesson.text: Note how the verbs change with the register. You **put** or **stick** a meal **on** your credit card informally, but you **charge it to** your credit card formally. A **direct debit** is a regular automatic payment; an **electronic transfer** moves money online between two accounts.

examples.text: Who shall I **make** this cheque **out to** / **payable to**?
examples.note: What name shall I put on it? payable to is slightly more formal

examples.text: The easiest way to pay your household bills is by **direct debit** or by **electronic transfer**.
Shall we **put**/**stick** this meal **on my credit card**? Then we can forget it.
Could you **charge it to my credit card**, please?

lesson.heading: Card vocabulary
rows: APR
annual percentage rate of interest, e.g. 'The APR for this card is 23%'
expiry date / to expire
the date after which the card is not valid, e.g. 'My card expires in 05/19'
credit card fraud
illegal use of someone's card or account
debit card
card where the money is taken directly from your bank account
store card
credit card issued by a shop for use in that shop
contactless card / payment
a payment made by touching the card or phone against the reader
PIN
personal identification number
ATM / cash machine / cashpoint
the machine you use to withdraw money

lesson.heading: Getting money out
lesson.text: You **withdraw** money from an account; informally you **get some money out**. If you type the wrong **PIN** too often, the machine may **swallow** your card.

examples.text: I went to **withdraw** some money / **get** some money **out** but I forgot my **PIN** and the **ATM** swallowed my card after three wrong attempts.
A lot of people don't like using **contactless cards** because they think they are more vulnerable to **fraud**. They prefer to use their phones to make **contactless payments**.
*A:* Is this a **credit card** or a **debit card**? *B:* Actually, it's a **store card**.

lesson.heading: Savings, pensions and investments
rows: a lump sum
a single, large payment, e.g. 'Victims will receive lump sum compensation payments.'
a golden handshake
a large payment made to someone on leaving a job
an annual bonus
an extra payment made once a year on top of a salary
a share portfolio
a combination of investments of different kinds
the stock market
the organisation which controls the buying and selling of parts of companies
stocks and shares
parts of the ownership of companies bought as investments
life savings
money saved over many years
a will
an official statement of what should happen to your money and property after your death
to cover the cost of something
to be enough money to pay for it
to borrow heavily / be deeply in debt
to take out large loans and owe a great deal

lesson.heading: Reading it in the news
lesson.text: These are the words you meet in financial news reports. Notice the collocations: compensation is **paid**, a handshake is **paid to** someone, debt is something you are **deeply in**, and money is **borrowed heavily**.

examples.text: A **golden handshake** of ten million pounds was **paid to** the boss of one of Britain's biggest companies today, in addition to an **annual bonus** of two million pounds.
People with well-managed **share portfolios** have done better on the **stock market** than individuals who buy **stocks and shares** privately.
Johan Carslow left only a very small sum to his family in his **will**. It was hardly enough to **cover** the cost of his funeral.
Ms Rafstedt had **borrowed heavily** to finance the building of a new house and found herself **deeply in debt**.

lesson.text: You **borrow** money from someone and you **lend** money to someone - a very common mistake is to say ~~lend from~~ a friend.

exercises.prompt: This is a credit card. If you want one that takes the money directly from your bank account, then you need a ___.
exercises.explanation: With a debit card the money leaves your account immediately.

exercises.prompt: I pay my rent by ___ every month, so I don't have to do anything.
exercises.explanation: A direct debit is a regular automatic payment from your account.

exercises.prompt: I couldn't pay for it last month as I was a bit ___ for cash.
exercises.explanation: To be strapped for cash is to need money and have very little.

exercises.prompt: I have to be very careful how I spend my money because things are a bit ___ right now.
exercises.explanation: If things are tight, your finances are not good at the moment.

exercises.prompt: You can now use your phone to make ___ payments on the bus and underground system in the city.
exercises.explanation: A contactless payment is made by touching the card or phone against the reader.

exercises.prompt: She never used her card on 9 April, but someone did and bought hundreds of pounds' worth of goods. It was a case of credit card ___.
exercises.explanation: Credit card fraud is the illegal use of someone's card or account.

exercises.prompt: I'm sorry, I can't lend you anything at all. I'm absolutely ___.
exercises.explanation: Broke (or the very informal skint) means having no money left.

exercises.prompt: When I ran out of money in Thailand, my parents made an ___ from their bank account to mine.
exercises.explanation: An electronic transfer is a movement of money online between two accounts.

exercises.prompt: I haven't got enough cash to pay for this meal; shall I just ___ it on my card?
exercises.explanation: Informally you put it or stick it on your card; formally you charge it to your card.

exercises.statement: She got a huge golden hand when she left the company.
exercises.explanation: She got a huge golden handshake when she left the company.

exercises.statement: My old aunt Jessie is rich in it. Every time I go to see her she gives me 100 pounds.
exercises.explanation: My old aunt Jessie is rolling in it. Every time I go to see her she gives me 100 pounds.

exercises.statement: My father got a lump sum when he retired, so he bought a weekend cottage.
exercises.explanation: Correct - a lump sum is a single, large payment.

exercises.statement: She put her living savings into an online company and lost everything when it collapsed.
exercises.explanation: She put her life savings into an online company and lost everything when it collapsed.

exercises.statement: If you need a very large sum of money, it's not a good idea to lend from friends or neighbours.
exercises.explanation: If you need a very large sum of money, it's not a good idea to borrow from friends or neighbours.
